"Keep abreast of" means to stay up-to-date with something — to continuously follow new information, changes, or developments about a topic so that you are never behind or left out.

Think of it this way: imagine you are walking side by side with a friend. You are matching their pace perfectly — not falling behind, not rushing ahead. That's exactly what this idiom means, but for information instead of walking. You are "walking alongside" the latest news or changes in something, never letting it get ahead of you.

Simple one-line meaning: To always know the latest about something.
Where Does It Come From? (Origin)

The word "abreast" is the key to understanding this idiom. It comes from the old nautical (sailing) and military world.

"Abreast" literally means side by side, at the same level. Soldiers marching in a line were said to be "abreast" of each other — all at the same position, no one ahead, no one behind.

Over time, people started using this word figuratively — not for people walking, but for keeping up with information. If you "keep abreast of" something, you are staying at the same level as the latest developments. You are not falling behind.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

"Keep" — to continue doing something consistently over time. Not just once, but as an ongoing habit.

"Abreast" — at the same level; side by side; not behind.

"Of" — this connects the action to the subject (what you are keeping up with).

So together: Keep + abreast + of = continuously stay at the same level as (something).
How Is It Used?

The structure is always: keep abreast of + [topic/subject]

You use it when talking about:

  • News and current events
  • Changes in a field or industry
  • Technology updates
  • Scientific research
  • Market trends
  • Any situation that is constantly changing
Examples in Real Life

Here are examples across many different contexts so you can see how natural and versatile this idiom is:

News and current events:
"She reads three newspapers every morning to keep abreast of what is happening in the world."

Technology:
"As a software developer, you must keep abreast of new programming languages and tools or your skills will become outdated."

Medicine:
"The doctor attends conferences every year to keep abreast of the latest research and treatments."

Business:
"The CEO keeps abreast of market trends to make smart decisions for the company."

Education:
"Good teachers keep abreast of changes in the school curriculum so their lessons stay relevant."

Personal life:
"I follow a few science pages on social media just to keep abreast of discoveries in space exploration."
The Tone and Register — Formal or Informal?

"Keep abreast of" leans slightly formal or professional. You will hear it often in:

  • Business writing and meetings
  • Journalism
  • Academic discussions
  • Professional conversations

It is not too formal — it is perfectly fine in everyday speech too. However, in casual conversation between friends, people might more naturally say "keep up with" instead. Both mean the same thing.

Formal context: "Employees are expected to keep abreast of company policy updates."
Casual version of the same idea: "Employees need to keep up with company policy updates."
Common Variations of This Idiom

The idiom appears in a few slightly different forms, all meaning the same thing:

"Stay abreast of" — identical in meaning to "keep abreast of." Both are correct and widely used.
Example: "He stays abreast of football transfers throughout the season."

"Keep someone abreast of" — this version means to inform or update another person about something. Notice how the object changes — now it's a person, not a topic.
Example: "Please keep me abreast of any new developments in the project."
(= Please inform me whenever something new happens.)

This second variation is very important because it flips the meaning slightly — instead of you following information yourself, you are giving updates to someone else.
"Keep Abreast Of" vs. Similar Idioms

These idioms are close in meaning but have subtle differences:

"Keep up with" — the most casual and common synonym. Means the same thing in most situations.
"I can't keep up with all the news."

"Stay on top of" — means not just following something, but actively managing or controlling it. It implies a slightly stronger effort.
"She stays on top of every new development in her department."

"Be in the loop" — means being included in a group of people who share important information. It focuses more on being included, not necessarily on effort.
"Make sure I'm in the loop about the meeting."

"Keep abreast of" sits right in the middle — it implies regular, conscious effort to follow changes, and it sounds educated and professional.
What Happens When You Don't "Keep Abreast Of" Something?

The opposite of keeping abreast of something is falling behind or being out of touch. English has idioms for that too:

  • "He has fallen behind on industry news."
  • "She is out of touch with current events."
  • "They were caught off guard because they didn't keep abreast of the changes."

Understanding the opposite helps you feel the full weight of the idiom — it highlights why keeping abreast of things matters.
A Quick Memory Trick

Picture a row of soldiers marching in a perfectly straight line — all at the same level, shoulder to shoulder, no one falling behind.

Now replace those soldiers with you and the latest information. You are marching right beside the news, the changes, the updates — always at the same level, never left behind.

That image is exactly what "keep abreast of" means.
